lessons.title: Basic Swirl Techniques: Drop, ITP, Hanger
lessons.body: Swirling is what turns plain soap into a product that sells for double. The three core techniques are drop swirl, ITP (in-the-pot) swirl, and hanger swirl. You need a loaf mould, a stick blender, and two or more colours of soap batter at light trace (like thin custard). Work in a cool room; if it's above 30Â°C, your batter may set too fast. In Africa, many soapers use wooden loaf moulds lined with plastic or silicone liners. For a drop swirl, pour a base colour into the mould, then pour contrasting colours from a height of about 30 cm in thin streams, moving back and forth across the length. The batter drops through the base, creating vertical streaks. For ITP, split your batter into cups, colour each, then pour all colours back into the main pot and give exactly three slow stirs with a spatulaâno more, or you'll muddle them. Pour the mixed batter into the mould. For a hanger swirl, pour your layers, then insert a bent wire hanger (or a thin dowel) and run it through the batter in an S-curve, up and down, once or twice. Don't overdo it. After pouring, bang the mould on the table to release air bubbles. Cover with cling film and insulate with a blanket. Gel phase helps colours pop. Unmould after 24â48 hours, cut into bars. Practice each technique with 500g batches of simple recipe: 350g olive oil, 150g coconut oil, 70g lye, 150g water. Master one swirl before moving to the next.

lessons.title: Layered and Gradient Soaps
lessons.body: Layered soaps are the easiest way to get a professional look. You pour one colour, let it set enough to support the next layer, then pour another. Gradient soaps are just many thin layers that fade from dark to light. You need a loaf mould, a stick blender, and a scale accurate to 1g. Work with a recipe that traces slowly: high olive oil (70%) and low coconut (30%) gives you time. For a basic two-layer soap, make your base batter, split it in two. Colour one part with 1 teaspoon of titanium dioxide dispersed in 1 tablespoon of oil for white, and the other with 1/2 teaspoon of charcoal for black. Pour the first layer, then wait 5â10 minutes until it forms a skin. You can speed this by putting the mould in the fridge for 5 minutes. Then pour the second layer gently over a spatula or the back of a spoon to avoid breaking the first layer. For a gradient, make 4â6 small batches of batter, each slightly lighter. Pour each layer, waiting 3â5 minutes between. Use a thermometer: batter should be 35â40Â°C. In hot African climates, work quickly and keep your mould cool. After the final layer, cover and insulate. Cut after 24 hours. If layers separate, your batter was too thin or too hot. If they blend, you waited too long. Practice with 500g batches.

lessons.title: Embedding Objects and Embeds
lessons.body: Embeds are pre-made soap pieces or small objects placed inside a new soap batch. They create surprise and texture. Common embeds: small soap balls, cubes, or shapes made from a previous batch; dried flowers like rose petals or lavender; and safe items like coffee beans or oats. Never embed fresh fruit, metal, or plasticâthey rot or leak. To make soap embeds, pour leftover batter into small silicone moulds, cure for 48 hours, then pop out. For a simple embed soap, make your main batter at light trace. Pour a 1 cm layer into the mould. Place your embeds on top, spacing them 2 cm apart. Then gently pour the rest of the batter over them. If embeds are light, they may floatâpush them down with a spatula. For a column embed, stand soap balls in a row along the mould. For a confetti embed, grate a cured bar of coloured soap and stir 1 tablespoon per 500g into your batter just before pouring. In Africa, dried hibiscus flowers or baobab seeds can be used if fully dried. After pouring, bang the mould to settle. Insulate and gel. Cut after 24 hours. If embeds fall out when cutting, they were too big or your batter was too cold. Keep embeds smaller than 2 cm.

lessons.title: Textured Tops and Stamps
lessons.body: Textured tops make soap look handmade and premium. You can create peaks, waves, or sprinkles. You need a spatula, a spoon, and optional tools like a fork or a stamp. Work when your batter is at medium traceâthick enough to hold shape. For peaks, pour your batter into the mould, then use a spatula to pull up the surface into little mountains. Let them set. For waves, drag a fork or a skewer through the top in a zigzag. For sprinkles, scatter dried herbs, oats, or poppy seeds over the wet top. In Africa, you can use dried moringa powder, cinnamon, or ground coffee. For stamps, you need a rubber or acrylic stamp with a design. Wait until your soap is firm but still slightly softâabout 12â24 hours after pouring. Press the stamp firmly into the top, then lift. If it sticks, dip the stamp in water first. You can also use a knife to carve lines or letters. For a glossy finish, spray the top with isopropyl alcohol (70%) after texturing. This prevents soda ash. After texturing, cover and insulate. Cut after 24 hours. If your peaks collapse, your batter was too thin. If your stamp smears, your soap was too soft. Practice on a small 500g batch.

lessons.title: Using Micas and Oxides
lessons.body: Micas and oxides are the safest and most vibrant colourants for soap. Micas are shimmering powders; oxides are matte pigments. You need a small digital scale (0.01g), a dedicated spoon, and a small cup. Always wear a mask when handling powders. For 500g of soap batter, use 1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon of mica or oxide. Too much can cause coloured lather or staining. To mix, put the powder in a cup, add 1 tablespoon of light oil (like sunflower), and stir into a smooth paste. Then add a spoonful of your soap batter and mix again. This prevents clumps. Add this slurry to your main batter and stick blend for 5 seconds. For swirls, separate your batter into cups and colour each cup individually. Popular African-inspired colours: red oxide for brick, yellow oxide for ochre, black oxide for charcoal, and mica for gold or copper. Note: some micas morph in high-pH soapâtest small batches. Oxides are stable. Do not use food colouring or craft glitter; they fade or irritate skin. Store powders in airtight containers away from humidity. Clean tools with paper towel first, then wash. If your colour fades, you used too little or the mica is not soap-safe. If it bleeds, you used too much. Start with 1/4 teaspoon per 500g.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Design Issues
lessons.body: Even experienced soapers get design failures. Here are the most common and how to fix them. 1) Soda ash: a white powdery film on top. Prevent by spraying 70% isopropyl alcohol on the surface after pouring, and covering with cling film. If it appears, steam it off or wash with warm water. 2) Cracked tops: your soap got too hot. This happens in hot African climates if you insulate too much. Uncover and cool, or reduce insulation. 3) Partial gel: a ring in the middle. Prevent by forcing gel (wrap in a towel) or preventing gel (put in fridge). Be consistent. 4) Swirls disappeared: your batter was too thick (heavy trace). Mix colours at light trace and work fast. 5) Layers separated: you poured too hot or too thin. Wait until a skin forms. 6) Embeds fell out: they were too large or your batter was too cold. Keep embeds under 2 cm. 7) Stamps smeared: soap was too soft. Wait 12â24 hours. 8) Colour faded: not enough colourant or not soap-safe. Use 1/2 teaspoon per 500g of oxide. 9) Air bubbles: bang the mould on the table before insulating. 10) Uneven cut: use a mitre box or a soap cutter. Always keep a notebook: record recipe, temperatures, colour amounts, and times. That is how you improve.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Design Techniques and Swirls for Soap Making

In Africa's fast-growing handmade soap sector â from Lagos to Nairobi, Accra to Cape Town â visual design is often the difference between a product that sits on a market table and one that sells out on WhatsApp and Instagram. A well-executed swirl or embed signals quality, justifies a premium price, and builds a recognisable brand. This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a single, business-ready guide. Use it alongside your supplier's safety data sheets (SDS) and your local cosmetics regulator's requirements.

Two principles underpin everything below: trace control and temperature control. Most design failures trace back to one of these. Master them and your swirls, layers, and embeds will behave predictably batch after batch â which is what allows you to scale from a home kitchen to a registered micro-enterprise.

1. Trace and Temperature: The Two Levers

Before any colour goes in, confirm your batter is at emulsion or very light trace for swirls, and medium trace for layers and embeds. In hot African climates (28â38 Â°C ambient), lye solution and oils cool slowly; aim for 30â35 Â°C for both. Cold batter thickens unpredictably; hot batter accelerates saponification and "seizes" your design. Keep a stick blender pulse count â 3 to 5 short pulses is usually enough for emulsion.

2. Basic Swirl Techniques: Drop, ITP, Hanger

  • Drop swirl: Pour coloured batter from height (20â30 cm) in a thin stream across the loaf. Works best at emulsion trace. Produces vertical, feathered columns.
  • In-the-Pot (ITP): Add 2â3 coloured portions into the main pot, give 1â2 slow stirs, then pour. Fast, repeatable, ideal for high-volume production runs.
  • Hanger swirl: After pouring, insert a bent wire hanger or silicone tool and sweep in S-curves. Best at medium trace so the batter holds the channel.

3. Layered and Gradient Soaps

Pour each layer at medium trace and let it set 3â5 minutes before the next. For gradients, split one batch into 4â6 cups and add increasing amounts of mica or oxide. In a warm workshop, work quickly â batter in the pot continues to saponify. A gradient that reads well in a 1 kg loaf may look flat in a 5 kg loaf; test at your target mould size.

4. Embedding Objects and Embeds

Embeds (soap balls, cubes, dried botanicals, melt-and-pour shapes) must be fully saponified and dry before use. Place them against the mould wall, then pour batter at light trace around them to avoid air pockets. Never embed fresh fruit, milk, or untreated botanicals â they rot and can grow mould.

5. Textured Tops and Stamps

Textured tops (spoon peaks, mica dusting, piped swirls) are applied within 5â10 minutes of pouring, while the surface is still soft. Stamps are pressed after unmoulding and curing â typically 24â48 hours for stamping, 4â6 weeks for full cure. Use food-grade or soap-safe stamp material and clean between batches to avoid cross-contamination.

6. Using Micas and Oxides

Cosmetic-grade micas and iron oxides are the workhorses of African soap design. Disperse powders in a little light oil (e.g., sweet almond or fractionated coconut) before adding to batter â never add dry powder directly, as it clumps. Typical usage: 1â2 tsp mica per 500 g of oils for strong colour; Â¼âÂ½ tsp for pastels. Iron oxides are stronger and more light-stable than many micas.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Lye (Sodium Hydroxide) Handling

Sodium hydroxide causes severe burns and permanent eye damage. Always wear chemical splash goggles, nitrile gloves, and long sleeves. Mix lye in a well-ventilated area â outdoors or under an extractor â and always add lye to water, never water to lye. Keep a bottle of white vinegar and clean running water within reach for spills. Store lye in a locked, labelled container away from children and food. In many African jurisdictions, soap making is regulated as a cosmetic manufacturing activity; check your national standards body (e.g., KEBS, SON, SABS, Ghana Standards Authority) for compliance requirements before selling.

7. Troubleshooting Design Issues

Table 1: Common Design Faults and Corrective Actions
Symptom Likely Cause Corrective Action
Swirls disappear / muddied colour Batter at heavy trace; over-stirred after colour added Stop at emulsion trace; stir max 2â3 times; pour immediately
Layers merge into each other Previous layer not set; batter too hot Wait 3â5 min between layers; cool batter to 30â32 Â°C
Air pockets around embeds Batter too thick; embeds not pre-wetted Pour at light trace; spritz embeds with alcohol; tap mould
Mica streaks / clumps Dry powder added directly Pre-disperse in 1 tsp light oil per colour
Colour fades after cure Non-lightfast dye or too little oxide Switch to iron oxides; store cured soap away from direct sun
Stamps smudge Soap too soft or too hard Stamp at 24â48 h; if too hard, mist surface lightly first
Soda ash on textured tops Exposed surface reacting with COâ Spritz 91% isopropyl alcohol on top; cover with cling film

Source: Adapted from Bramble Berry Soap Queen troubleshooting guides (2023) and HSCG member technical bulletins (2022).

8. Colourant Reference Table

Table 2: Micas and Oxides â Usage and Behaviour
Colourant Typical Dosage (per 500 g oils) Best Use Notes for African Markets
Cosmetic mica (fine) 1â2 tsp Swirls, gradients, mica dusting Widely imported; check for cosmetic-grade certification
Iron oxide (red, yellow, black) Â¼âÂ½ tsp Layers, embeds, strong colours Locally available via cosmetic suppliers in Lagos, Nairobi, Accra
Ultramarine blue Â¼âÂ½ tsp Cool tones, ocean themes Stable in CP soap; avoid in acidic additives
Chromium oxide green Â¼ tsp Natural-look greens Very stable; popular for herbal-positioned lines
Titanium dioxide Â½â1 tsp Whitening, pastel base Use dispersible grade to avoid speckling
Activated charcoal 1â2 tsp Black/grey swirls, "detox" positioning Locally sourced; can accelerate trace â work fast

Source: Dosage ranges compiled from Bramble Berry colourant guides (2023) and the EU CosIng cosmetic ingredient database (2024).

9. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. PPE on: goggles, nitrile gloves, long sleeves, closed shoes.
  2. Lye solution cooled to 30â35 Â°C; oils at same temperature.
  3. Batter at emulsion or light trace before adding colour.
  4. Colourants pre-dispersed in light oil â never added dry.
  5. Embeds fully cured, dry, and at room temperature.
  6. Work in a cool, shaded area during hot African afternoons.
  7. Label every batch with date, recipe code, and fragrance/colour used.
  8. Cure 4â6 weeks in a ventilated, dark space before selling.

10. Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Handcrafted Soap & Cosmetic Guild (HSCG) â free technical bulletins and safety resources.
  • U.S. FDA Cosmetics Guidance â labelling and safety reference.
  • EU CosIng Database â official cosmetic ingredient and colourant listings.
  • ISO 22716:2007 â Good Manufacturing Practices for cosmetics.
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â local cosmetic compliance for East African producers.

Business note: Design consistency is a commercial asset. Document every swirl, layer, and colour ratio in a batch log. When a design sells well on Jumia, Takealot, or at your local market, you can reproduce it exactly â and that reproducibility is what turns a craft into a brand.

quiz.q: What is the correct trace stage for a drop swirl?
quiz.explanation: Light trace allows the batter to flow and create distinct swirls without blending together.

quiz.q: How many slow stirs should you give an ITP swirl after adding colours back to the pot?
quiz.explanation: Three stirs combine colours without muddling them into a single shade.

quiz.q: What tool is traditionally used for a hanger swirl?
quiz.explanation: A bent wire hanger is inserted and moved in an S-curve to create the swirl pattern.

quiz.q: In a layered soap, how long should you wait between layers?
quiz.explanation: Waiting 5â10 minutes allows a skin to form so the next layer doesn't break through.

quiz.q: What oil percentage helps slow trace for gradient soaps?
quiz.explanation: High olive oil slows trace, giving more time to pour multiple layers.

quiz.q: Which of these is safe to embed in soap?
quiz.explanation: Dried botanicals are safe; fresh items rot and metal or plastic can leak or irritate skin.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended size for soap embeds?
quiz.explanation: Embeds larger than 2 cm may fall out when cutting or cause uneven bars.

quiz.q: How can you make confetti embeds?
options: A) Grate a cured bar of coloured soap
D) Pour hot batter over ice
quiz.explanation: Grating cured soap creates small pieces that mix into the batter as confetti.

quiz.q: What trace stage is best for textured tops?
quiz.explanation: Medium trace is thick enough to hold peaks but still workable.

quiz.q: What can you spray on soap to prevent soda ash?
quiz.explanation: Isopropyl alcohol helps the surface set evenly and reduces ash formation.

quiz.q: When stamping soap, how long should you wait after pouring?
quiz.explanation: Soap needs to firm up but still be slightly soft for a clean stamp impression.

quiz.q: What is a common African ingredient for texturing soap tops?
quiz.explanation: Dried moringa powder is a safe, locally available botanical for sprinkling.

quiz.q: How much mica or oxide is recommended per 500g of soap batter?
quiz.explanation: 1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon gives vibrant colour without staining or fading.

quiz.q: What should you mix mica with before adding to soap batter?
quiz.explanation: Mixing with a light oil creates a smooth slurry that prevents clumps.

quiz.q: Which colourant is known to morph in high-pH soap?
quiz.explanation: Some micas are not stable in high-pH environments and change colour.

quiz.q: What is a safe alternative to craft glitter in soap?
quiz.explanation: Mica provides shimmer without the environmental and skin risks of plastic glitter.

quiz.q: What causes soda ash on soap?
options: B) Unsaponified lye reacting with air
quiz.explanation: Soda ash forms when free lye reacts with carbon dioxide in the air.

quiz.q: How can you fix a cracked soap top?
quiz.explanation: Cracks come from overheating; uncovering and cooling prevents further damage.

quiz.q: What is partial gel?
options: A) A ring in the middle of the soap
quiz.explanation: Partial gel happens when the centre gels but the edges do not, creating a ring.

quiz.q: Why might your swirls disappear?
quiz.explanation: Thick trace prevents colours from flowing and blending into distinct swirls.

quiz.q: What should you do before insulating a mould to remove air bubbles?
options: B) Bang the mould on the table
quiz.explanation: Banging the mould releases trapped air bubbles that can cause holes.

quiz.q: What is the best way to record your soap designs?
quiz.explanation: Keeping a notebook of recipes, temperatures, and times helps you repeat successes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that your layers might separate?
options: C) You used too much colour
D) You used a silicone mould
quiz.explanation: Pouring too hot can melt the previous layer and cause separation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature range for soap batter when layering?
quiz.explanation: 35â40Â°C is warm enough to pour smoothly but not hot enough to melt layers.

quiz.q: What can you use to create waves on a soap top?
quiz.explanation: Dragging a fork through the top creates a wavy texture.

quiz.q: Which oxide gives a brick-red colour?
quiz.explanation: Red oxide is commonly used for brick or terracotta shades.

quiz.q: How should you store mica and oxide powders?
options: B) In airtight containers away from humidity
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers prevent clumping and contamination from moisture.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to embed dried hibiscus flowers?
options: B) Ensure they are fully dried
quiz.explanation: Only fully dried botanicals are safe; fresh ones can rot or cause discolouration.

quiz.q: What causes embeds to fall out when cutting?
quiz.explanation: Large embeds create weak spots and may dislodge during cutting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of spraying isopropyl alcohol on a textured top?
quiz.explanation: Alcohol helps the surface set evenly and reduces soda ash formation.
